clue.text: Flying ace meets tennis champ in town

indicators.note: one name meeting the other means the two sit side by side in a row

parts.note: Biggles is the fictional fighter pilot hero of W. E. Johns's boys' adventure books
Virginia Wade won the Wimbledon women's singles title in 1977

explanation.surface: A star pilot encounters a tennis winner somewhere in a provincial town.
explanation.walkthrough: The town is in Bedfordshire, England. Biggles's creator was W. E. Johns, which explains the puzzle's four clues about Johns.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a market town in Bedfordshire, England, so it is an example of a town.

clue.text: "Strictly" does it for Rambo — LOL!

parts.note: read the first word of the answer as anagram fodder and the second as its indicator: its eight letters rearranged spell RAMBOLOL, the clue's Rambo and LOL

explanation.surface: A joking remark that the BBC dance show is just the thing for the action hero Rambo, laughing out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse anagram: the answer is the instruction and the clue words are its result. Strictly Come Dancing is a BBC television show of celebrity couples competing on the dance floor.
explanation.definitionFit: The television show Strictly Come Dancing is a contest in waltzes, tangos and foxtrots, the formal partner style it showcases.

clue.text: Filled out a complaint, say

indicators.note: 'say' tells us the word is spoken, so we want the word that is pronounced the same

parts.note: a groan is a moan or grumble of complaint

explanation.surface: Someone completed a complaint form, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filled out' looks like completing a form, but it means got bigger, as a growing child does.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has filled out has put on size and become mature, which is what having matured physically means.

clue.text: Delete one broadcast — it's Gone With The Wind, currently

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: An instruction to cut a single transmission, with a nod to the famous film.
explanation.walkthrough: The film title is the trap: 'currently' points to a water current, so the definition is a tidal stream going the same way as the wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A tide flowing in the same direction as the wind blows is the sailors' term for this, so its current goes with the wind.

clue.text: Follow first of delinquents before stuttering copper's turned up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the whole string is read from the bottom upwards
before puts the first piece ahead of the second in the line

parts.note: the first letter of delinquents is D, here written out as the name of the letter, DEE
copper is Cu, its chemical symbol; stuttering repeats the first sound, C-CU, and the 's adds S

explanation.surface: A tale of a young offender ahead of a stammering policeman who has arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' reverses everything, DEE plus CCUS read upwards. 'copper' looks like a police officer, but it is the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: To follow someone in an office or role is to come after them and take their place, a synonym.

clue.text: Holding hands — get off, OK?

indicators.note: holding means the outer word keeps the other piece inside it

parts.note: to alight is to get off a bus or train
the two hands are left and right, L and R

explanation.surface: Someone holding hands is told to let go, and asked whether that is acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hands' looks like palms held together, but it means left and right, L and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean satisfactory or acceptable, so they are synonyms and either can be asked as a question.

clue.text: One that wrote of Irish rights, including related English issue

indicators.note: including means the first pieces wrap around the rest

parts.note: Erse is the Irish Gaelic language
people related to you are your kin
issue means offspring, a child
R stands for right, so two of them are RS

explanation.surface: A writer on Irish rights deals with a family matter involving the English.
explanation.walkthrough: The Irish piece and the rights piece run together, then split after their third letter to take the inner run. The author was also an Irish nationalist, executed in 1922, so the surface fits him.
explanation.definitionFit: Erskine Childers wrote The Riddle of the Sands, the 1903 spy novel, so he is someone who wrote.

clue.text: One that hits on the cuddly type in secret

indicators.note: on means one piece is added on to the other, so the second piece comes after the first

parts.note: someone who likes to cuddle is fond of embracing people
a street robber who attacks and hits people

explanation.surface: Somebody who flirts with an affectionate person does it on the quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hits on' reads as flirting, but 'One that hits' is the robber and 'on' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The reduplicated phrase is an old idiom for secrecy or concealment, so in its adverb use it means covertly.

clue.text: Hippy movement using horses, reportedly, in Western Isles and Wales (never the South)

indicators.note: the South is S, the abbreviation for south, and never means every S is taken out of the islands and Wales
using means the island letters take the sounded horses into service inside them
reportedly means we take how the word sounds rather than how it is spelt

parts.note: gee-gees is a childish name for horses, which sounds like the two letters G G

indicators.note: in means a second pair of the sounded letters sits inside Wales as well

explanation.surface: A description of horses being used to move about the Scottish islands and Wales, but never in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horses, reportedly' supplies its pair of letters to both halves. The Western Isles are the Outer Hebrides of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A swaying, wobbling motion of the hips is exactly the kind of movement the reduplicated word describes.

clue.text: Release John and Bob in a foreign setting

indicators.note: in puts the toilet and the coin inside the foreign word
the foreign word forms a setting, like a mount round a jewel, for the other letters

parts.note: une is French for a, the indefinite article
john is slang for a toilet, as is loo
a bob was a shilling in old British money, abbreviated S

explanation.surface: Two men are being freed while abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: John and Bob look like two men's names, but John is a toilet and Bob is the old shilling, a coin worth twelve pence before 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: To release something is to set it free or slacken it, which is what this rare intensive form of loose means.

clue.text: Huge statues: unfinished seconds, originally Italian

indicators.note: unfinished means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: the punctuation mark printed after statues is a colon
s is the abbreviation for second, so two of them are SS

indicators.note: originally tells us to take only the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A note about giant sculptures left incomplete, the second-rate ones being from Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon after 'statues' is part of the wordplay: the punctuation mark's name, cut short, starts the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the plural of the word for a giant statue, like the one that once stood at Rhodes.

clue.text: Verbal adjective in "poor undeserving pair of Poles dismissed"

indicators.note: poor tells us the remaining letters are in a bad, disordered state and must be rearranged
dismissed means these letters are removed from the word

parts.note: the two poles are North and South, N and S

explanation.surface: A quoted phrase describing a needy couple from Poland being sent away.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing N and S from 'undeserving' leaves UDEERVING, which is then rearranged. 'Poles' looks like people from Poland but means the magnetic poles.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin grammar this form is an adjective made from a verb, expressing what must be done, as in agenda.

clue.text: Soprano's profession, reportedly self-confessed, is killing

indicators.note: reportedly means we want the word that sounds like what is said

parts.note: a soprano's job, confessed in her own words, is 'I sing'

explanation.surface: Tony Soprano, the TV mob boss, admits his line of work is murder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'self-confessed' turns the soprano's job into her own words, 'I sing'. Icing is US gangster slang for murder; The Sopranos is an American TV series about the Mafia.
explanation.definitionFit: To ice someone is gangster slang for murdering them, so the noun is underworld slang for a murder.

clue.text: Small jumper? Medium? John's the smallest

parts.note: a roo is a kangaroo, especially a young one, which jumps
M is the size abbreviation for medium

explanation.surface: Questions about a sweater's size, then a remark that John's is the smallest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumper' looks like a sweater, as do the clothing sizes, but it is a leaping animal. A john is a toilet, which British English calls the smallest one in the house as a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a toilet is 'the smallest' chamber in a house, so the definition completes that familiar joking phrase.

clue.text: Principal thing for a poser to say: "It's all brawn in LA"

parts.note: a principal of a school is its head

parts.words: thing for a poser to say
parts.note: people posing for a photo are told to say cheese to make them smile

explanation.surface: A main photographer's cue, with a joke that Los Angeles is all about muscle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brawn' looks like muscle, but it is the British name for jellied meat from a pig's head; Americans give it this other name.
explanation.definitionFit: In American English this is the name for brawn, a cold cut of pork pressed in its own jelly.

clue.text: Short-lived navy beheaded John, perhaps

parts.note: a navy is a nation's fleet of ships

indicators.note: beheaded means the first letter is cut off

parts.note: King John was an English monarch, so John is an example of a king

explanation.surface: A navy briefly executed a man called John.
explanation.walkthrough: King John reigned in England from 1199 to 1216, and the 'perhaps' tells us he is one example of a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that passes very quickly is brief and transient, which is what short-lived means.

clue.text: Model beaten up in poorly lit backstreet nearest the centre

indicators.note: in means the rearranged letters sit inside the other pieces

parts.note: poorly lit is DIM, which back turns round, followed by ST for street

indicators.note: beaten up means knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fashion model is attacked in a dark alley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backstreet' must be split: 'back' turns round the word for poorly lit, and 'street' gives its usual abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of middle means placed most centrally, so a synonym for being closest to the middle point.

clue.text: See 7
Fool is at first taken in by damsel in distress

indicators.note: taken in by means the letter goes inside the other word
distress means agitation, so the letters are in disorder and must be rearranged
at first means only the opening letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A fool is initially fooled by a damsel who needs rescuing.
explanation.walkthrough: The damsel's letters are rearranged to make MSLEAD, and the I from 'is' goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to fool someone is to deceive or trick them, a synonym.

clue.text: Wrong about function taken by daughter substitute

indicators.note: about means the first word goes around the others

parts.note: a sin is a wrong

indicators.note: taken by means accompanied by, so the second piece follows on after the first

parts.note: tan, short for tangent, is a trigonometric function

explanation.surface: A misdeed concerning a social event attended by someone's daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'function' looks like a party, but it is the mathematical tangent.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who stands in for another, an understudy or replacement, is a substitute.

clue.text: What upset John — possibly …

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone asks what upset John, and the clue runs on into the next one.
explanation.walkthrough: The actor John Thaw played Inspector Morse on British TV; 'possibly' marks the name as one example. The ellipsis carries John into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: John Thaw was the English actor in Inspector Morse, so the definition is a first name standing for its famous surname.

clue.text: See 8
… his bottom being pinched by Richard in class?

indicators.note: being pinched by means held tightly inside another piece

parts.note: Richard Gere is the American film actor

indicators.note: the bottom of a word is its last letter

parts.note: his refers back to the John of the previous clue

explanation.surface: Continuing the last clue, John gets his backside pinched by Richard in a lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'his' points back to John in the previous clue, whose last letter is N. 'class' looks like a school lesson but means a category.
explanation.definitionFit: A category or kind of artistic work, such as crime fiction or jazz, is a class of that art.

clue.text: Part of car where electrician briefly has trailer attached

indicators.note: having something attached means it is joined on at the end
having something attached means it is joined on at the end
briefly means the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: Sparks is a nickname for an electrician
a trailer advertises something, and so does a plug

explanation.surface: A garage tells you where an electrician has hooked on a trailer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trailer' looks like a towed cart, but it is a promotional advert, as is a plug.
explanation.definitionFit: This device in a petrol engine gives the spark that ignites the fuel, so it is one component in a vehicle.

clue.text: King lying in state? That is for Requiem Mass, partly

parts.note: KY is the postal abbreviation for Kentucky, a US state
R stands for rex, Latin for king
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A dead monarch lies in state, which is the reason for a funeral mass, in part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lying in state' looks like a royal funeral, but it puts R inside KY.
explanation.definitionFit: This 'Lord have mercy' prayer is one section of the Mass, including the Requiem, so it is part of one.

clue.text: Surprised if Iceland keeps building

indicators.note: keeps means the words hold the answer inside them, running across their boundaries

explanation.surface: Someone is astonished that Iceland holds on to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'building' looks like a verb about to complete the sentence, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An edifice is a large, imposing structure, so this is a synonym for a construction.

clue.text: Perhaps reading or writing about boring, boring writer

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so the pieces go inside

parts.note: something boring is dull
reading and writing are two of the three Rs of schooling, so either is an R
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A dismissive review of a tedious author's reading and writing.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'boring' means drilling into, the second means dull. The three Rs are reading, writing and arithmetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence and Gerald Durrell were both authors, so the surname belongs to a writer.

clue.text: Late-night "entertainers" mangling Gay Gordons outside church? Not unknown!

indicators.note: outside means the rearranged letters wrap around the church letters
mangling means crushing out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
Y is a classic unknown quantity in algebra, and 'not' means it is removed

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Nightclub dancers butchering a Scottish country dance around a church.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gay Gordons is a Scottish country dance. Remove Y, rearrange GAGORDONS to GOGODANRS, and put CE inside.
explanation.definitionFit: These are dancers hired to perform energetically in nightclubs, so they are entertainers at late-night venues.
